definition: A unit of data size: 10^18 bytes, or 1,000 petabytes. Only the very largest storage systems reach this scale.
example: Adding 6–8 PB a day for a year is about 2–3 EB.

definition: A binary unit of data size: exactly 1,024 bytes (2^10). It exists to avoid confusion with the kilobyte, which is 1,000 bytes.
example: RFC 9309 asks crawlers to parse at least the first 500 KiB (512,000 bytes) of a robots.txt file.

definition: A unit of data rate: one million bits per second. Network speeds and video bitrates are quoted in bits, so divide by 8 to get megabytes per second.
example: A 10 Mbps video stream sends 1.25 megabytes every second, or 4.5 GB an hour.

definition: The value below which a given percentage of measurements fall. p99 latency is the time that 99% of requests beat; the slowest 1% take longer. It describes the experience of unlucky users better than the average does.
example: If p99 hold latency is 1.5 s, one hold in a hundred takes longer than 1.5 s.

definition: A unit of compute: one processor core busy for one hour. Dividing core-hours of work per day by 24 gives the number of cores that must run around the clock.
example: 10.8 million core-hours a day needs about 450,000 cores running non-stop.

definition: The amount of work in progress at the same moment: requests open, users active or jobs running at once. It differs from throughput, which counts work completed per second.
example: 1,000 fetches a second that each take 1 second means about 1,000 requests in flight.

definition: Taking incoming data into a system: receiving uploads, location updates or events and writing them somewhere for processing.
example: 500,000 location updates of 100 bytes each is 50 MB/s of ingest.

definition: A single key, row, partition or account that receives far more traffic than the rest, so it overloads its one server or lock no matter how big the cluster is. The usual fixes are caching, splitting it into sub-keys, or batching.
example: A viral video whose view counter is one database row becomes a hotspot taking thousands of increments a second.

definition: Running a system in several geographic cloud regions so it survives a regional outage and serves users nearby. Keeping data consistent across regions adds latency and complexity, so designs often give each record one home region for writes.
example: A ticketing system can serve its catalogue from every region while each event's seat inventory lives in one home region.

definition: A physical frame holding many servers that often share power and a network switch, so they can fail together. Placing replicas on different racks protects against that.
example: Plan about 100 nodes rather than the 75-node minimum so losing a whole rack still leaves enough capacity.

definition: Non-Volatile Memory Express: an interface that connects SSDs directly to the processor over PCI Express, giving much lower latency and higher throughput than older disk interfaces.
A Linux Foundation body that hosts open-source infrastructure projects such as Kubernetes, etcd and Vitess.
Capitalised requirement words in RFCs, defined by RFC 2119: MUST is an absolute requirement, SHOULD is a strong recommendation that may be ignored only for good, understood reasons.
example: RFC 9309 says a crawler SHOULD NOT use a cached robots.txt for more than 24 hours.

definition: How many bits per second an encoded video stream uses, usually in Mbps. Higher bitrate means more detail but more storage and bandwidth.
example: A 1080p H.264 stream might use about 5 Mbps; a 4K stream about 15 Mbps.

definition: The set of renditions a video is encoded into, from low resolution and bitrate to high. Each step is a "rung" that an adaptive player can climb or drop to.
example: 240p at 0.3 Mbps up to 2160p at 15 Mbps.

definition: The most widely supported video codec, standardised in 2003. Almost every device can decode it in hardware, so platforms encode it first for fast, universal playback.
Google's royalty-free video codec, released in 2013, used heavily by YouTube. It typically needs fewer bits than H.264 at similar quality, at a higher encoding cost.

A royalty-free video codec released in 2018 by the Alliance for Open Media (whose members include Google, Netflix and Amazon). It compresses better than VP9 and H.264 but is slower to encode, so platforms use it for popular content.

A video frame stored complete, without reference to other frames, so decoding can start there. Other frames store only changes, so keyframes cost more bits; streaming segments normally start with one so each can be decoded on its own.

A run of video frames starting with a keyframe, followed by frames that depend on it. In a closed GOP no frame refers outside the group, so the video can be cut there and each piece decoded on its own.
A file format that wraps encoded video, audio and metadata together, such as MP4 or MPEG-TS. The container is separate from the codec used inside it.
A common video container format. Fragmented MP4 (fMP4) splits the file into self-contained fragments, which suits streaming in short segments.
An older container designed for broadcast, used by the original versions of HLS. Newer HLS deployments can use fragmented MP4 instead.
A high-quality intermediate master copy of a video, lightly compressed so it has quality to spare, from which all the delivery renditions are transcoded.

A small text file that lists a video's renditions and the URLs of their segments. The player downloads the manifest first, then chooses which segments to fetch. HLS uses .m3u8 playlists; DASH uses an XML MPD.

Streaming where the video is encoded at several bitrates and split into segments, and the player picks the best rendition for each segment based on its network speed and buffer. It avoids stalls on slow links without wasting quality on fast ones.
The XML manifest used by MPEG-DASH to list a video's renditions and segments.
A standard format for fragmented-MP4 media segments that both HLS and DASH players can use, so one set of segment files can serve both protocols when codecs and encryption match.
Playing a single video file while it downloads over HTTP. It cannot change quality mid-stream, so it stalls on slow networks.
When playback pauses because the player's buffer of downloaded video has run out. Viewers find it far more annoying than lower quality.
Video downloaded ahead of the playback position, measured in seconds. A full buffer lets the player ride out network dips without stalling.
example: With 30 s buffered, a 4 s network dip does not cause a stall.

definition: An adaptive-bitrate approach, studied by Netflix researchers, that picks the bitrate mainly from how full the playback buffer is rather than from noisy throughput measurements. Throughput-based players instead choose from recent download speed.
Requiring sustained evidence before changing state, so a value near a threshold does not flip back and forth. In video players it stops quality jumping between rungs on every noisy measurement.
An Amazon S3 feature that uploads a large object as separately numbered parts, which can be sent in parallel and retried individually, then combined by a final "complete" call.
An HTTP header saying which bytes of a whole resource a request or response carries, for example bytes 0–8388607 of a file. Resumable uploads use it to send the next chunk.
An open-source system, built at YouTube, that shards MySQL across many servers while presenting it to applications much like one database. It is a CNCF graduated project.
A physical location where many networks connect and exchange traffic with each other directly, avoiding paid transit.
Google servers placed inside ISP networks that cache popular Google content, such as YouTube video, close to users.
A cache that fetches an object from the layer behind it on the first request (a miss), stores it, and serves later requests itself. Nothing is placed in advance.
Loading content into caches before anyone asks for it, based on predicted demand, typically during quiet hours when bandwidth is cheap.
Embedding or linking to another site's files directly so they are served from that site's bandwidth. Expiring signed URLs prevent it.
Technology that encrypts media and controls which devices may decrypt it, using keys from a licence server. Widevine (Google), FairPlay (Apple) and PlayReady (Microsoft) are the common systems.
Google's DRM system, used on Android, Chrome and many smart TVs.
Apple's DRM system, used with HLS on Apple devices.
Microsoft's DRM system, used on Windows, Xbox and many TVs.
A service that checks whether a device may play protected content and, if so, gives it the decryption key.
A database's record of changes written before they are applied to data files, so committed changes can be replayed after a crash. It is a form of write-ahead log.
An older streaming protocol originally from Macromedia/Adobe Flash. It is still widely used to send live video from an encoder to a streaming platform's ingest servers.
An open-source protocol for sending live video over unreliable networks with low latency, often used for contribution feeds into a live-streaming ingest tier.
Video Multimethod Assessment Fusion: a video quality metric developed by Netflix that predicts how good viewers would judge a video, used to tune encoding.
Choosing encoding settings for each video (per title), or each scene (shot-based), instead of one fixed bitrate ladder for everything. Simple content gets fewer bits for the same quality.
Cheaper, slower storage for data that is rarely read. Moving old data to colder tiers cuts cost at the price of slower access.
Apple's protocol for streaming audio and video from an Apple device to a TV or speaker.
Extensible Markup Language: a text format for structured data using nested tags, such as the DASH MPD manifest.
The fourth generation of mobile data networks (LTE). Its speed varies widely as you move, so streaming must adapt.
Automated checks run on uploads, such as comparing against fingerprints of copyrighted material or using classifiers to detect unsafe content.
The two angles that locate a point on Earth: latitude measures north–south from the equator (−90° to 90°), longitude east–west from the prime meridian (−180° to 180°).
Writing binary data using 32 different characters, each standing for 5 bits.

In grid-based spatial indexes, two points very close together can fall in different cells, so a search of only one cell misses nearby results. Searching every cell that overlaps the search area, then filtering by real distance, fixes it.
A tree that recursively splits a 2D area into four quarters until each leaf holds at most a set number of points. It adapts to density, with small cells where points are crowded.

Google's library that projects the Earth onto the six faces of a cube and divides each face into a hierarchy of square-ish cells, numbered along a Hilbert curve, with 64-bit ids and 31 levels (0 to 30).
Uber's open-source geospatial index that tiles the Earth with hexagons (plus 12 pentagons per resolution) at 16 resolutions, 0 to 15. Each finer resolution has cells about one seventh the area.
example: Resolution 8 cells average about 0.74 km².

definition: A tiling of the plane with six-sided cells. Each hexagon has six neighbours that all share an edge, so distances to neighbours are roughly equal; a sphere cannot be tiled by hexagons alone, so H3 also uses 12 pentagons per resolution.
A solid with 20 triangular faces. H3 projects the Earth onto one before laying out its hexagons.
All H3 cells within k steps of a centre cell. It holds 1 + 3 × k × (k + 1) cells: 7 for k = 1 and 19 for k = 2.
A space-filling curve that visits every cell of a grid in an order where cells close along the curve are close in space, so a 2D area maps to a few ranges of a 1D index.
A space-filling curve made by interleaving the bits of the coordinates, which is what geohash does. It preserves locality less well than a Hilbert curve, jumping at some boundaries.
The predicted time for a driver to reach a pickup, computed by routing over the road network with live traffic. It is a better ranking signal than straight-line distance.
Finding the fastest path between two points over a graph of roads, with edges weighted by travel time. It is far more expensive than a straight-line distance calculation.
State that can be lost and rebuilt from fresh input, such as driver locations refreshed every few seconds, so it does not need durable storage or backups.
Data that is short-lived and only useful briefly, such as live cursor positions or the latest location. It is kept in memory and never written to durable logs.
An open-source Node.js library from Uber that let application servers share work across a consistent-hash ring, using the SWIM gossip protocol for membership.
The exchange of messages at the start of a TLS connection in which client and server agree keys. It costs one or more round trips, so reusing connections saves time.
An atomic operation that changes a value only if it still equals what you expect, for example "set offered only if state is still available". Of two concurrent attempts, exactly one succeeds.
A number that increases each time ownership or leadership changes. Stamping requests with it lets a store reject work from an older, stale owner.
Assigning each request immediately to whatever looks best right now, such as the nearest driver. It is fast but can produce worse results overall than considering several requests together.
Collecting requests for a short window (a second or two) and assigning them together to minimise total cost, such as total pickup time, at the price of a little added delay.
Matching a set of agents (drivers) to tasks (riders) one-to-one so the total cost is as small as possible, given a matrix of costs for every pair.
A classic algorithm that solves the assignment problem exactly in polynomial time (O(n^3) for n agents in common versions).
A network-optimisation problem: send a required amount of flow through a graph at the lowest total cost. Matching problems can be expressed this way.
Planning routes for a fleet of vehicles to serve many pickups and drop-offs at minimum cost. It is much harder than one-to-one matching.
Raising prices in an area when demand outstrips supply, expressed as a multiplier on the normal fare, to encourage more drivers and dampen demand.
A stored price offered to a customer with an id and an expiry time. Honouring it until expiry keeps the price the rider saw even if surge changes a moment later.
The fraction of the truly relevant items that a search or filter keeps. A distance shortlist with low recall drops the driver with the best ETA.
A starting address given to a crawler; everything else it finds is reached by following links from the seeds.
A link from a page to another page. Each fetched page typically yields dozens of outlinks, so discovered URLs grow much faster than fetched pages.
The crawler's queue of URLs waiting to be fetched, organised so that it picks important pages first while never hitting one host too fast.

A scalable web crawler built at Compaq research in the late 1990s. Its frontier design uses priority "front queues" feeding per-host "back queues", with a heap of next-allowed fetch times for politeness.
The rules a crawler follows so it does not overload websites: obey robots.txt, make at most about one request at a time to a host, and wait between requests.
A text file at the root of a website (/robots.txt) telling crawlers which paths they may fetch, using User-agent, Allow and Disallow lines. RFC 9309 (2022) standardised it.
robots.txt lines that permit or forbid paths by prefix. Under RFC 9309 the matching rule with the most octets wins, and Allow wins a tie.
example: /shop/help/returns matches both "Disallow: /shop" and "Allow: /shop/help"; the longer Allow wins.

definition: Exactly 8 bits. Network standards say octet rather than byte to be unambiguous.
A non-standard robots.txt line some sites use to ask for a minimum number of seconds between requests. It is not part of RFC 9309, but polite crawlers honour it.
A standard file format (ISO 28500) for storing many raw web responses with their headers in one large file, used by the Internet Archive and Common Crawl.
A non-profit that crawls the web and publishes the data openly, in WARC files, for anyone to use.
A non-profit digital library that archives web pages over time, viewable through the Wayback Machine.
Google's original algorithm that scores a page's importance by the number and importance of pages linking to it. Crawlers use such scores to decide what to fetch first.
Rewriting URLs into one standard form so that different spellings of the same address count as one: lower-casing the scheme and host, removing default ports and fragments, and resolving ../ segments.
example: HTTP://Example.com:80/a#top and http://example.com/a normalise to the same URL.

definition: The part of a URL after #, which points within a page and is never sent to the server.
The "." and ".." parts of a URL path, meaning "this folder" and "the parent folder". Clients resolve them before sending a request.
An HTML hint in which a page names its preferred URL, so search engines can treat duplicates as one. It is a hint, not proof the pages are identical.
A short value computed from content, such as a hash, used to recognise the same or similar content without comparing it byte by byte.
A fingerprinting method (Charikar's) where similar documents get fingerprints differing in only a few bits. Google used 64-bit SimHash with a 3-bit threshold to find near-duplicate web pages.
A technique for quickly estimating how similar two sets are (their Jaccard similarity), often used on sets of word shingles to find near-duplicate documents.
The number of positions at which two equal-length strings of bits differ.
example: 1011 and 1001 have a Hamming distance of 1.

definition: If more items are put into boxes than there are boxes, some box holds at least two. In SimHash lookup: 3 differing bits spread over 4 blocks leave at least one block identical.
Pages whose content is almost the same, for example differing only in an advert or a timestamp. Exact hashes miss them; similarity fingerprints like SimHash catch them.
A site structure that generates an endless supply of distinct URLs, such as a calendar with a "next month" link forever, which can trap a naive crawler.
Doing input/output without blocking a thread while waiting: the program starts many network operations and is notified as each completes, so a few threads can handle thousands of connections.
A Linux system call interface that lets one thread efficiently watch thousands of sockets and learn which are ready to read or write.
Many small websites served from one machine and often one IP address, so per-site rate limits can still add up to overload that machine.
A file in which a website lists its URLs, often with last-modified dates, to help crawlers find and refresh pages.
A protocol that lets websites notify participating search engines immediately when pages are added, changed or deleted.
Running a page in a real browser engine (often without a screen, "headless") so content built by JavaScript appears. It costs far more CPU and memory than fetching raw HTML.
A hostname is a full name like shop.example.com; the registered domain is the part bought from a registry (example.com); the top-level domain (TLD) is the last label (.com).
The start of a URL: the scheme (https) and the authority (host plus optional port, such as example.com:443). Each default port (80 for http, 443 for https) is implied when omitted.
Capping requests to one IP address, as well as to each hostname, so many sites sharing one server are not overloaded together.
A large ticket-selling company. Its Verified Fan programme pre-registers buyers and sends codes to a selected group before a sale.
The moment tickets for an event go on sale, when huge numbers of buyers arrive at once for limited inventory. An earlier on-sale restricted to registered or invited fans is called a presale.
A temporary reservation of seats for one buyer while they pay, with an expiry time after which the seats return to sale.
Locking rows before reading and changing them (for example with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE), so other transactions wait. It is safe but makes contended rows queue up.
The four conditions that must all hold for a deadlock: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no pre-emption, and circular wait. Always acquiring locks in one fixed order removes circular wait.
Options of the Redis SET command: NX sets the key only if it does not exist yet; PX gives it an expiry in milliseconds.
example: SET seat:e1:14F h1 NX PX 480000 holds a seat for 480,000 ms (8 minutes).

definition: Asking the card issuer to approve and reserve an amount on a card without moving money yet. It is later captured or released, and lapses after some days if not captured.
Completing an authorised card payment so the money is actually taken. Capture can happen immediately or later, for example when a ride ends.
Cancelling an authorisation before it is captured, releasing the reserved funds.
Tickets without assigned seats, so inventory is just a count of tickets remaining.
Splitting one hot counter or balance into N separate rows and choosing one per update, so updates spread across rows; read the total by summing them.
example: 20,000 tickets as 50 rows of 400 each.

definition: Making a client solve a small computational puzzle before it is served, which costs a human little but makes mass automated requests expensive.
Identifying a device from combined attributes such as browser, screen and settings, used to limit one person to one queue position.
A design from the LMAX exchange in which one thread processes all events for some state in memory, in order, with durable input logs for recovery, avoiding locks entirely.
A component that owns some state and handles messages for it one at a time, so no locks are needed for that state.
A background job that periodically finds expired records, such as old seat holds, and tidies them up. Correct designs do not depend on it running on time.
A region that shares a local time, including its daylight-saving rules. The IANA time zone database names them (such as Europe/London) and records their history.
Moving clocks forward in spring and back in autumn. Some local times are skipped on the spring change and happen twice on the autumn change, which schedulers must handle explicitly.
example: In the UK, 01:00–02:00 local time does not exist on the last Sunday in March.

definition: The UK's winter time, equal to UTC.
The UK's summer time (BST), one hour ahead of UTC, from the last Sunday in March to the last Sunday in October.
The world's reference time, with no daylight saving. Storing instants in UTC avoids ambiguity; a UTC offset such as +01:00 is how far a local time is ahead.
A job that runs once at a set time, as opposed to a recurring job that runs on a schedule.
A system that runs jobs at specified times or intervals and tracks their outcomes.
Loading work a little before it is needed, such as jobs due in the next 5 seconds, so it can be dispatched on time.
A primary key made of several columns together, such as (job_id, scheduled_at), so each combination may appear only once.

A circular array of time slots, each holding the timers due then; a pointer advances one slot per tick. Hierarchical wheels add coarser wheels for minutes and hours. Kafka uses them for delayed operations.
A queue that hides a message until a set delay has passed. Amazon SQS allows delays of up to 15 minutes (900 seconds).
An AWS service for running one-off or recurring tasks at a set time, suited to delays longer than SQS allows.
A Kubernetes object that creates Jobs on a cron schedule. startingDeadlineSeconds limits how late a missed run may start; concurrencyPolicy (Allow, Forbid or Replace) controls overlapping runs.
Serving several queues in turn, in proportion to their weights, so no single queue's backlog starves the others.
An open-source durable-execution platform: workflow code is replayed from recorded history after failures, while activities (side effects) are retried.
An open-source platform for scheduling and monitoring batch workflows defined as DAGs of tasks.
A company that lets merchants accept card and other payments, talking to card networks and banks on their behalf. Stripe, Adyen and Braintree are examples.
A payment service provider owned by PayPal.
Returning some or all of a captured payment to the customer. It is recorded as a new transaction, never by editing the original one.
A forced reversal of a card payment started by the cardholder's bank after a dispute, for example over fraud or goods not received.
The actual movement of funds after a payment, when the provider pays the merchant (minus fees). Providers publish settlement reports listing what they settled.
Money sent from a platform or payment provider to a bank account, such as a seller's daily earnings.
The two sides of a double-entry record. A debit increases assets and expenses; a credit increases liabilities and revenue. Many systems store debits as positive and credits as negative numbers.
Categories of ledger account: assets are what you hold or are owed, liabilities what you owe (such as a driver payable), revenue what you earn, expenses what you spend.
A temporary account holding money in transit, such as funds a payment provider owes you but has not paid out yet. A non-zero balance shows money still in flight.
A new ledger transaction that cancels an earlier one, used instead of editing history so the audit trail stays complete.
A currency's smallest unit, such as pence for pounds. Storing amounts as whole numbers of minor units keeps money arithmetic exact. Most currencies have 2 decimal places, but JPY has 0 and BHD has 3.
The international standard of three-letter currency codes (GBP, EUR, JPY, BHD) and the number of decimal places each uses.
The UK currency; 1 pound (£) = 100 pence.
The euro, the currency of most EU countries, with 2 decimal places (cents).
The Japanese yen, which has no minor unit in practice: amounts are whole yen.
The Bahraini dinar, divided into 1,000 fils, so it has 3 decimal places.

The standard for floating-point arithmetic. Its binary64 (double) format cannot represent most decimal fractions exactly, so 0.1 + 0.2 gives 0.30000000000000004. The standard also defines decimal formats.
A number type that stores base-10 digits exactly with a fixed scale, such as SQL NUMERIC, avoiding binary floating-point rounding.
Replacing a card number with a meaningless token. The provider's hosted form or SDK collects the card, and your systems only ever see the token.
An extra card-payment authentication step, where the cardholder confirms with their bank (for example in a banking app). Its result often arrives asynchronously.
A record that fails to match between your ledger and an external source during reconciliation.
The networks that move money, such as card schemes, bank transfer systems and open banking (bank-to-bank payments started through bank APIs).
A multi-step process made of local transactions, where a failure is handled by running compensating steps that undo earlier ones, instead of one big distributed transaction.
An open-source database designed specifically for double-entry financial transfers under high contention.
A stored precomputed value, such as an account balance, kept updated for fast reads even though it could be recomputed from underlying entries.
A payment state for when a provider call timed out and you cannot tell whether it succeeded. It is resolved by querying the provider or retrying with the same idempotency key, never by guessing.
A fraud signal based on how many attempts a card, device or account makes in a short time.
A hash of a request body stored with its idempotency key, so a reused key with a different request can be detected and rejected.
A complete, tamper-resistant record of who did what and when, used to explain every balance.

A technique for real-time co-editing in which edits are index-based operations (insert at position 5) and a concurrent operation is transformed against others, shifting its positions, so every copy ends up the same. Google Docs used a server-ordered form.
All replicas reaching an identical state once they have seen the same operations. It says nothing about whether the merged result is what users meant.
In collaborative editing, the property that an operation has the effect its author intended (my insert lands where I put it) even after concurrent edits.
Showing a user's own edit immediately on their screen before the server confirms it, so typing never waits for the network.
An ordered, append-only list of every edit operation applied to a document. Replaying it from a snapshot rebuilds any revision.
A number identifying a document version; each committed operation increases it by one, giving a total order of edits.
The one server that owns a document at a time, holding it in memory, ordering incoming edits, logging them and broadcasting them to collaborators.

Correctness conditions for OT transform functions. TP1: two concurrent operations give the same result whichever order they are transformed and applied. TP2: transforming against sequences in different orders also agrees; it is notoriously hard to satisfy and is avoided by server-ordered designs.
One component that puts all operations into a single order, such as a per-document server in OT.
Delivering messages so that if one operation could have influenced another, every replica receives the first before the second.
A sequence CRDT for text in which each insert references the id of the character it follows.
A text CRDT by Weidner and Kleppmann designed to avoid interleaving concurrent insertions character by character.
A research CRDT from Ink & Switch for rich text, handling formatting such as bold spans across concurrent edits.
A merge result where two users' concurrently typed words are mixed character by character, such as "cdaotg" from "cat" and "dog".
Apps that keep the main copy of data on the user's device and work fully offline, syncing with others when connected, typically using CRDTs.
Peer-to-peer: devices exchange data directly without a central server.
A browser-based design tool whose multiplayer editing uses a server-authoritative model with last-writer-wins per object property.
A list stating who may read or edit a resource. Servers must check it on every operation, including ones sent after reconnecting.
Rewriting a list of local operations so they apply on top of changes made elsewhere in the meantime.
An editor feature where changes are proposed for others to accept or reject instead of being applied directly.
N is the number of replicas of a key, W how many must acknowledge a write, R how many must answer a read. If R + W > N, every read group overlaps every write group in at least one replica.
example: N = 3, W = 2, R = 2 overlaps and tolerates one replica down.

definition: A fast non-cryptographic hash function; Cassandra uses it to map partition keys to 64-bit tokens on its ring.
The circular range of hash values in consistent hashing. Each node owns positions (tokens) on it, and a key belongs to the next nodes clockwise from its hash.
The node handling a client request in a leaderless store; it forwards to the replicas and waits for enough responses.
Sending a duplicate request to another replica when the first is slower than usual, to cut tail latency.
Version A descends from (dominates) version B when A's vector clock is at least B's in every entry and bigger in one, so B can be discarded.
A Cassandra column type that supports increment and decrement which merge across replicas, avoiding read-modify-write; retries are not idempotent.
A well-known node that a new node contacts first to join the cluster's gossip.
How much extra work storage does: read amplification is files touched per read, write amplification is bytes rewritten per byte written, space amplification is disk used per byte of live data.

Cassandra compaction strategies: size-tiered (STCS) merges similar-sized files, good for writes but needs headroom; leveled (LCS) keeps sorted levels for reads; time-window (TWCS) groups data by time so expired files drop whole.
Adding a node to a cluster by streaming its share of data from existing replicas.
All rows sharing one partition key, stored together on the same replicas. Oversized partitions hurt compaction, repair and memory.
A client library that knows the ring layout and sends each request straight to a replica owning the key, saving a hop.
A Cassandra replication setting that sets the number of replicas in each data centre separately.
Asking a replica for a hash of its data instead of the data itself, to check agreement cheaply.

Spreading scheduled jobs over an allowed window by giving each job a fixed offset computed from a hash of its id, so the fleet is spread out but each job keeps a regular interval. Random jitter instead picks a new random offset each time.
example: offset = hash(job_id) % 300 seconds spreads 2 million hourly jobs over 5 minutes.

definition: A Redis command that returns members of a geospatial sorted set within a radius or box of a point. Redis stores the locations as 52-bit geohash scores.
A Redis command that returns sorted-set members whose scores fall in a range, for example every job whose due timestamp is before now.
The file (and command) listing a Unix machine's cron jobs. Each line is a cron expression of five fields (minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week) followed by a command.
example: "0 9 * * MON-FRI" means 09:00 every weekday; "0 * * * *" means minute 0 of every hour.

definition: An open-source tool that schedules and runs Cassandra repairs in small segments so they do not overload the cluster.
Yet Another Transformation Approach: the sequence-CRDT algorithm used by the Yjs library to order concurrent insertions.
Reusing one TCP (and TLS) connection for several HTTP requests instead of opening a new connection for each, saving handshake round trips.
A URL carrying an expiry time and a cryptographic signature that a CDN checks before serving, so links to protected video segments stop working after a while and cannot be hot-linked forever.
A stable identifier for one scheduled occurrence of a job, usually built from the job id and the scheduled time. Workers and downstream services use it to deduplicate repeated attempts.
example: (job j9, 2026-10-01T09:00Z) always gives the same run id however many times it is fired.

definition: The identifier of the grid cell (geohash, S2 or H3) that contains a location. Indexing drivers by cell id turns "who is nearby?" into looking up a few cells.
The record of every URL a crawler has already queued or fetched, checked before adding a newly discovered link. It can be an exact store, a Bloom filter, or both.
A cap on how many pages a crawler fetches from one host per crawl cycle, scaled by the host's importance, which bounds the damage from spider traps.
How often a page's content changes, estimated from fetch history and used to decide how often to re-crawl it.
A cursor or selection position stored relative to a stable element id rather than as a numeric offset, so it stays attached to the same text when others edit before it.
A cheap first check that rejects most candidates before an expensive or authoritative step, such as a Redis hold before the database conditional update, or straight-line distance before road routing.
An operation that either completes fully or has no effect at all, such as holding all four requested seats or none.

A storage-heavy server in Netflix's Open Connect CDN that stores and serves Netflix video. Netflix supplies OCAs to qualifying ISPs to install inside their networks, or places them at internet exchange points, so most video bytes travel only a short distance.

Low-Latency HLS: an extension of Apple's HTTP Live Streaming for live video. It divides the newest media into short partial segments that can be packaged and published before their full parent segment is finished, so players can stay closer to the live edge.

A Cloudflare product that holds excess visitors on a static queue page in front of a website and lets them in at a configured rate, protecting the origin during traffic spikes such as ticket on-sales.
A commercial virtual-waiting-room service that places surging visitors in an online queue and admits them to a site at a controlled rate.

In an LSM-tree store such as Cassandra, background work that merges several immutable SSTable files into new ones, keeping only the newest version of each value and dropping data whose tombstones are old enough. It bounds how many files a read must check, but needs spare disk space while it runs.
example: Cassandra's size-tiered strategy can temporarily need as much free space again as the SSTables it is merging.
